cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-16-christ.summary: A small bust of the Christ-Logos holding a scroll appears in the middle of the sky and turns toward the bearded psalmist, who stands on top of a fiery furnace holding up two pairs of scales. The furnace comes from the Latin 'igne me examinasti' ('thou hast tried me with fire'), and an angel shelters him with outspread wings from the enemies on either side. The drawing renders the psalm's plea for judgement and protection almost like a diagram.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-16-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

walters:W.44.25R.summary: The risen Christ, holding a cross-staff, steps out of a gabled doorway and grasps the wrist of a naked figure, pulling the righteous dead from the gaping jaws of a great grey Hell-mouth. Above, grotesque demon heads peer over a crenellated wall. The vivid scene shows the old Christian belief that Christ descended to the dead and freed Adam, Eve and the righteous.
facts: The Harrowing of Hell (fol. 25r) faces the Three Marys at the Tomb (fol. 24v) in the 14th-century prefatory cycle of Walters W.44.
The monstrous, animal-headed Hell-mouth is a characteristic motif of northern Gothic art.
The story is not told in the Gospels; it rests on brief New Testament allusions and the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus.

walters:W.44.25R.notes: The Walters online record dates this leaf with the whole manuscript to the third quarter of the 13th century, but the Walters' own manuscript description (TEI, The Digital Walters) states that the ten full-page miniatures of the prefatory cycle (fols. 18v–27r) were added in the fourteenth century; the date is corrected accordingly. The worklist year (750) was a parsing error. The 'old Christian belief' is stated generally; the Gospel of Nicodemus link is standard and summarised in the linked Wikipedia article.

Q128910.summary: Leonardo captures the instant after Christ announces that one of the twelve will betray him: the apostles recoil, question and protest in groups of three, while Christ sits calm and still at the centre, framed by the window behind him. The painting's psychological drama and perfect perspective made it one of the most famous images in Western art.
facts: Leonardo painted in tempera on a sealed dry wall rather than in true fresco so he could work slowly and revise, but the paint began to flake within a few decades.
All the lines of the room's perspective converge at Christ's head.
It was commissioned by Duke Ludovico Sforza as part of his renovation of the convent; a doorway cut through the wall in 1652 destroyed Christ's feet.
A painstaking restoration, from 1978 to 1999, took more than twenty years.
